questions.question: Which chamber of the heart receives deoxygenated blood from the systemic circulation?

options.explanation: The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins.
The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood to the systemic circulation.
The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood via the superior and inferior venae cavae.
The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the pulmonary circulation.
The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood away from the heart.

explanation.overview: The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood via the superior and inferior venae cavae.
explanation.highYield: Right atrium = deoxygenated blood from body. Left atrium = oxygenated blood from lungs.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Increased right atrial pressure can be a sign of right heart failure or fluid overload.

questions.question: The tricuspid valve is located between the:

options.explanation: The tricuspid valve separates the right atrium from the right ventricle.

options.text: Superior vena cava and right atrium
options.explanation: No valve exists there; the SVC enters the right atrium directly.

explanation.overview: The tricuspid valve separates the right atrium from the right ventricle.
explanation.highYield: Tricuspid valve = right AV valve. Three leaflets. Prevents backflow during systole.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Tricuspid regurgitation can cause jugular venous distention and pulsatile liver.

questions.question: The bicuspid (mitral) valve prevents backflow from the:

options.explanation: The mitral valve closes during ventricular systole, preventing regurgitation into the left atrium.
It opens to allow flow from atrium to ventricle.

explanation.overview: The mitral valve closes during ventricular systole, preventing regurgitation into the left atrium.
explanation.highYield: Mitral valve = left AV valve. Two leaflets. Closure produces S1.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Mitral regurgitation causes a holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla.

questions.question: The pulmonary valve is located between the:

options.explanation: The pulmonary semilunar valve guards the exit from the right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk.

explanation.overview: The pulmonary semilunar valve guards the exit from the right ventricle into the pulmonary trunk.
explanation.highYield: Pulmonary valve = right semilunar valve. Opens during systole, closes during diastole (P2 of S2).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Pulmonary valve stenosis causes a systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border.

questions.question: The aortic valve opens when left ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure during:

options.explanation: Once ventricular pressure exceeds aortic diastolic pressure, the aortic valve opens, beginning ejection. This occurs after isovolumetric contraction.
The valve opens before rapid ejection; opening marks the end of isovolumetric contraction.
Atrial systole occurs during ventricular diastole.
During filling, the AV valves are open, not the aortic valve.

explanation.overview: Once ventricular pressure exceeds aortic diastolic pressure, the aortic valve opens, beginning ejection.
explanation.highYield: Aortic valve opens at the end of isovolumetric contraction, when LV pressure > aortic diastolic pressure.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Aortic stenosis impedes valve opening, increasing afterload and leading to left ventricular hypertrophy.

questions.question: The first heart sound (S1, 'lub') is produced by:

options.explanation: S1 occurs at the beginning of systole when the mitral and tricuspid valves close.
Ventricular filling is silent; a third heart sound (S3) may be heard in some conditions.
Atrial contraction can produce S4 if stiff ventricle.

explanation.overview: S1 occurs at the beginning of systole when the mitral and tricuspid valves close.
explanation.highYield: S1 = closure of AV valves (mitral + tricuspid). Best heard at apex. Marks start of systole.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Loud S1 may occur in mitral stenosis; soft S1 in mitral regurgitation or heart failure.

questions.question: The second heart sound (S2, 'dub') is associated with:

options.text: Closure of aortic and pulmonary valves
options.explanation: S2 occurs at the end of systole when the semilunar valves close.
AV valve opening is normally silent.

explanation.overview: S2 occurs at the end of systole when the semilunar valves close.
explanation.highYield: S2 = closure of aortic (A2) and pulmonary (P2) valves. Physiologic splitting on inspiration.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Wide fixed splitting of S2 is classic for atrial septal defect.

questions.question: A split S2 that widens on inspiration is commonly heard in:

options.explanation: Physiological splitting of S2 occurs during inspiration due to increased venous return delaying pulmonic valve closure.
ASD causes a wide fixed split, not variable with respiration.
Pulmonary stenosis can cause a wide split, but usually not as variable.
Aortic stenosis does not typically cause a widened split S2.
Mitral regurgitation does not affect S2 splitting.

explanation.overview: Physiological splitting of S2 occurs during inspiration due to increased venous return delaying pulmonic valve closure.
explanation.highYield: Physiologic S2 split: A2 then P2, wider during inspiration. Expiration: split narrows or disappears.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Absence of splitting may indicate a fixed obstruction (e.g., severe pulmonary hypertension).

questions.question: The P wave on an ECG represents:

options.explanation: The P wave reflects spread of depolarization through the atria.
Ventricular depolarization is the QRS complex.
Atrial repolarization is usually hidden within the QRS.
Ventricular repolarization is the T wave.
The PR segment reflects AV nodal delay.

explanation.overview: The P wave reflects spread of depolarization through the atria.
explanation.highYield: P wave = atrial depolarization. Absent in atrial fibrillation. Peaked P in right atrial enlargement; notched P in left atrial enlargement.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: A prolonged P wave duration can indicate interatrial block.

questions.question: The QRS complex corresponds to:

options.explanation: The QRS complex represents rapid depolarization of the ventricles.
AV nodal conduction occurs during the PR segment.
Bundle branch depolarization is part of the QRS, but the QRS overall is ventricular depolarization.

explanation.overview: The QRS complex represents rapid depolarization of the ventricles.
explanation.highYield: QRS = ventricular depolarization. Normal duration <120 ms. Wide QRS = bundle branch block or ventricular rhythm.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Q waves may indicate prior myocardial infarction if deep and wide.

questions.question: The T wave on an ECG represents:

options.explanation: The T wave corresponds to repolarization of the ventricles.
Atrial repolarization is usually hidden by QRS.
Purkinje activity is part of the QRS.
SA node firing is not visible on surface ECG.

explanation.overview: The T wave corresponds to repolarization of the ventricles.
explanation.highYield: T wave = ventricular repolarization. Inverted T waves may indicate ischemia. Peaked T waves in hyperkalemia.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: T wave inversions in specific leads can localize areas of ischemia or past infarction.

questions.question: The PR interval measures the time from:

options.text: Atrial depolarization onset to ventricular depolarization onset
options.explanation: PR interval includes atrial depolarization and conduction delay through the AV node.

options.text: SA node firing to atrial depolarization
options.explanation: SA node firing is not seen on ECG.
The PR interval includes the AV delay plus atrial depolarization.

options.text: QRS onset to T wave end

explanation.overview: PR interval includes atrial depolarization and conduction delay through the AV node.
explanation.highYield: Normal PR = 0.12-0.20 s. Prolonged PR = first-degree AV block. Short PR may indicate pre-excitation (WPW).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: A progressively lengthening PR then dropped QRS is second-degree AV block type I (Wenckebach).

questions.question: A prolonged PR interval (>200 ms) indicates:

options.explanation: First‑degree AV block is a delay in AV conduction, manifest as PR prolongation.
Third-degree block is complete AV dissociation.
Bundle branch block widens the QRS.
Ventricular hypertrophy causes increased QRS voltage.

explanation.overview: First‑degree AV block is a delay in AV conduction, manifest as PR prolongation.
explanation.highYield: PR > 200 ms = first-degree AV block. Usually benign; may be caused by increased vagal tone, medications (beta‑blockers, digoxin).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: First-degree AV block rarely requires treatment but may progress if due to structural disease.

questions.question: The QT interval represents:

options.text: Total duration of ventricular depolarization and repolarization
options.explanation: QT interval encompasses ventricular electrical systole, from QRS start to T wave end.
The QT interval approximates the ventricular action potential duration.

options.text: Time from QRS onset to T wave end
options.explanation: That is the definition, but all options are essentially true; the original answer was 'All of the above'.
QT interval encompasses ventricular electrical systole, from QRS start to T wave end.
It does represent depolarization and repolarization.

explanation.overview: QT interval encompasses ventricular electrical systole, from QRS start to T wave end.
explanation.highYield: QTc = QT corrected for heart rate (Bazett: QTc = QT/√RR). Normal QTc < 440 ms males, < 460 ms females. Prolonged QT → torsades risk.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Many drugs (antiarrhythmics, antibiotics, psychotropics) can prolong QT. Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia also prolong QT.

questions.question: The normal heart rate is set by the:

options.explanation: The SA node is the primary pacemaker due to its fastest intrinsic firing rate.
The AV node is the secondary pacemaker, slower than SA node.
The bundle of His can act as a pacemaker if higher centers fail.
Purkinje fibers are the slowest intrinsic pacemaker.
Ventricular myocytes are not pacemaker cells under normal conditions.

explanation.overview: The SA node is the primary pacemaker due to its fastest intrinsic firing rate.
explanation.highYield: SA node intrinsic rate: 60-100 bpm. AV node: 40-60 bpm. Purkinje: 15-40 bpm.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Sick sinus syndrome can result in bradycardia and pauses, requiring pacemaker.

questions.question: The intrinsic firing rate of the AV node is approximately:

options.explanation: That is the Purkinje fiber rate.
The AV node typically fires at 40‑60 bpm if the SA node fails.
That is the upper end of normal SA node rate.

explanation.overview: The AV node typically fires at 40‑60 bpm if the SA node fails.
explanation.highYield: AV node backup pacemaker. Junctional escape rhythm at 40-60 bpm when SA node fails.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Accelerated junctional rhythm (>60 bpm) can occur in digitalis toxicity or myocardial ischemia.

questions.question: Purkinje fibers have an intrinsic rate of:

options.explanation: Purkinje fibers are the slowest intrinsic pacemakers, firing at 15‑40 bpm.
That is the AV node rate.
That is the lower SA node rate.

explanation.overview: Purkinje fibers are the slowest intrinsic pacemakers, firing at 15‑40 bpm.
explanation.highYield: Ventricular escape rhythm: 15-40 bpm, wide QRS. Life-saving when higher pacemakers fail.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Complete heart block with ventricular escape may present with bradycardia and fatigue.

questions.question: The plateau phase (phase 2) of the ventricular action potential is mainly due to:

options.explanation: Ca2+ entry through L‑type channels balances K+ efflux, creating the plateau.
Na+ influx is responsible for phase 0.
K+ efflux occurs but is balanced by Ca2+ influx.
Chloride currents play a minor role.
The exchanger contributes later to Ca2+ removal.

explanation.overview: Ca2+ entry through L‑type channels balances K+ efflux, creating the plateau.
explanation.highYield: Phase 2 (plateau) = L‑type Ca2+ current. Allows sustained contraction. Blocked by calcium channel blockers.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: The plateau is critical for excitation-contraction coupling; Ca2+ entry triggers SR Ca2+ release.

questions.question: Phase 0 of the cardiac action potential in ventricular myocytes is caused by:

options.text: Rapid Na+ influx through voltage‑gated channels
options.explanation: Fast Na+ channels open, causing rapid depolarization (phase 0).
Na+ efflux occurs via Na+/K+ ATPase, not phase 0.

explanation.overview: Fast Na+ channels open, causing rapid depolarization (phase 0).
explanation.highYield: Phase 0 = rapid Na+ influx (INa). Blocked by class I antiarrhythmics. Fast conduction velocity.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Loss of Na+ channel function slows conduction (e.g., ischemia, hyperkalemia).

questions.question: In SA nodal cells, the upstroke (phase 0) is produced by:

options.explanation: SA node cells lack fast Na+ channels; depolarization is Ca2+-dependent via L‑type channels.
Pacemaker cells lack fast Na+ channels.
Funny channels contribute to diastolic depolarization, not phase 0.
SR release amplifies Ca2+ but does not generate the upstroke.

explanation.overview: SA node cells lack fast Na+ channels; depolarization is Ca2+-dependent via L‑type channels.
explanation.highYield: SA node phase 0 = L‑type Ca2+ current. Slower upstroke than ventricular cells. Targeted by calcium channel blockers.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Verapamil and diltiazem can slow SA node rate and are used for rate control in atrial fibrillation.

questions.question: The funny current (If) in pacemaker cells is carried by:

options.explanation: If is a mixed Na+/K+ inward current activated by hyperpolarization, contributing to diastolic depolarization.
It is mixed, not purely Na+.

explanation.overview: If is a mixed Na+/K+ inward current activated by hyperpolarization, contributing to diastolic depolarization.
explanation.highYield: If = 'funny' current. Activated by hyperpolarization. Enhanced by sympathetic (β1) stimulation. Inhibited by ivabradine.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Ivabradine selectively blocks If channels, slowing heart rate without affecting contractility, used in heart failure and angina.

questions.question: Sympathetic stimulation increases heart rate by:

options.text: Increasing If and L‑type Ca2+ currents
options.explanation: Norepinephrine enhances If and ICa,L, steepening the pacemaker potential.

explanation.overview: Norepinephrine enhances If and ICa,L, steepening the pacemaker potential.
explanation.highYield: Sympathetic: β1 → ↑ cAMP → ↑ If, ICa,L → faster phase 4 depolarization, ↑ HR. Also ↑ contractility.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Beta‑blockers oppose sympathetic effects, reducing HR and contractility, beneficial in CAD and heart failure.

questions.question: Parasympathetic (vagal) stimulation slows heart rate by:

options.text: Increasing K+ conductance (hyperpolarization) and decreasing If
options.explanation: ACh activates GIRK channels, hyperpolarizing the cell, and inhibits adenylyl cyclase, reducing If.
It reduces Ca2+ current indirectly via cAMP reduction.
It hyperpolarizes, making it harder to reach threshold.

explanation.overview: ACh activates GIRK channels, hyperpolarizing the cell, and inhibits adenylyl cyclase, reducing If.
explanation.highYield: Parasympathetic: M2 receptor → ↑ K+ efflux (hyperpolarization), ↓ cAMP → ↓ If, ICa,L → ↓ HR.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Vagal maneuvers (carotid sinus massage, Valsalva) can terminate AV node‑dependent tachycardias.

questions.question: The absolute refractory period of cardiac muscle prevents:

options.explanation: The long refractory period ensures the heart relaxes between beats, preventing tetanus.
Premature beats can occur if the stimulus arrives after the absolute refractory period.

explanation.overview: The long refractory period ensures the heart relaxes between beats, preventing tetanus.
explanation.highYield: Absolute refractory period (ARP): no stimulus can generate another action potential. Prevents summated/tetanic contractions, allowing rhythmic pumping.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Shortening of refractory period can predispose to reentrant arrhythmias.

questions.question: Cardiac output is defined as:

options.text: Mean arterial pressure / total peripheral resistance
options.explanation: That is Ohm's law analogy: CO = MAP / TPR.

explanation.overview: Cardiac output (L/min) = HR × SV.
explanation.highYield: CO = HR × SV. Normal ~5 L/min at rest. Cardiac index = CO / BSA (2.5-4 L/min/m²).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Low CO leads to hypotension, fatigue, and organ hypoperfusion.

questions.question: Stroke volume is primarily determined by:

options.explanation: Preload, afterload, and myocardial contractility are the three main determinants of stroke volume.
Heart rate affects CO but not SV directly.
EDV is preload, but SV also depends on afterload and contractility.
ESV is the residual volume after contraction.
Venous return influences preload, but other factors matter.

explanation.overview: Preload, afterload, and myocardial contractility are the three main determinants of stroke volume.
explanation.highYield: SV determinants: preload (Frank‑Starling), afterload (inversely related), contractility. SV = EDV - ESV.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: In heart failure, preload is increased but contractility is decreased, reducing SV.

questions.question: Preload refers to:

options.explanation: Preload is the initial stretch of cardiac myocytes, best measured as end‑diastolic volume or pressure.
Aortic diastolic pressure is a component of afterload.
MAP is determined by CO and TPR.
CVP reflects right atrial pressure, an indicator of preload but not preload itself.

explanation.overview: Preload is the initial stretch of cardiac myocytes, best measured as end‑diastolic volume or pressure.
explanation.highYield: Preload = EDV or EDP. Increased by venous return. Frank‑Starling: ↑ preload → ↑ SV.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Excessive preload in heart failure leads to pulmonary congestion.

questions.question: Afterload is best defined as:

options.text: The tension the ventricle must develop to eject blood
options.explanation: Afterload is the load against which the ventricle contracts, approximated by aortic pressure.
Aortic systolic pressure is a clinical correlate but afterload is the wall stress during ejection.
That is afterload for the right ventricle.
Compliance is the change in volume for a given pressure change.

explanation.overview: Afterload is the load against which the ventricle contracts, approximated by aortic pressure.
explanation.highYield: Afterload = ventricular wall stress during ejection. Increased in hypertension, aortic stenosis. Chronic ↑ afterload → hypertrophy.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Reducing afterload with vasodilators improves stroke volume in heart failure.

questions.question: According to the Frank‑Starling law, an increase in end‑diastolic volume results in:

options.explanation: Greater preload stretches sarcomeres, optimizing actin‑myosin overlap and increasing force.
Bainbridge reflex may increase HR, but Frank‑Starling increases SV.
Contractility is independent; the relationship describes increased force due to stretch.

explanation.overview: Greater preload stretches sarcomeres, optimizing actin‑myosin overlap and increasing force.
explanation.highYield: Frank‑Starling: ↑ EDV → ↑ SV (intrinsic property). Mechanism: optimal overlap of actin/myosin, increased Ca2+ sensitivity.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: In dilated heart failure, the heart operates on a flatter part of the Frank‑Starling curve; increased preload no longer increases CO.

questions.question: Ejection fraction is calculated as:

options.explanation: That would be the complement, not EF.

explanation.overview: Ejection fraction (normal ≈55‑70%) = SV / EDV.
explanation.highYield: EF = (EDV - ESV)/EDV × 100%. Reflects systolic function. HFrEF = EF ≤40%. HFpEF = EF ≥50%.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: EF is a key prognostic indicator post‑MI; low EF increases risk of sudden cardiac death.

questions.question: A positive inotropic agent increases contractility by:

options.explanation: Positive inotropes (e.g., digoxin, catecholamines) enhance Ca2+ cycling, increasing force.
SERCA inhibition would reduce Ca2+ reuptake and impair relaxation.

explanation.overview: Positive inotropes (e.g., digoxin, catecholamines) enhance Ca2+ cycling, increasing force.
explanation.highYield: Positive inotropy: ↑ intracellular Ca2+ (increased influx, SR release, or decreased efflux). Examples: β‑agonists, digoxin, phosphodiesterase inhibitors.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Dobutamine is a β1‑agonist used for short‑term inotropic support in cardiogenic shock.

questions.question: The dromotropic effect refers to changes in:

options.explanation: Dromotropy affects conduction speed, especially through the AV node.

explanation.overview: Dromotropy affects conduction speed, especially through the AV node.
explanation.highYield: Dromotropy = conduction velocity. Positive dromotropy: catecholamines speed AV conduction. Negative: adenosine, calcium channel blockers, digoxin (at toxic doses).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: AV nodal blocking agents (e.g., verapamil) are used to control ventricular rate in atrial fibrillation.

questions.question: The chronotropic effect refers to changes in:

options.explanation: Chronotropy affects the rate of SA node depolarization.

explanation.overview: Chronotropy affects the rate of SA node depolarization.
explanation.highYield: Positive chronotropy: sympathetic stimulation, β‑agonists. Negative: parasympathetic, β‑blockers, calcium channel blockers.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Ivabradine is a pure negative chronotrope (If channel blocker) used in heart failure and angina.

questions.question: The diagram shows a Wiggers diagram. Which wave corresponds to atrial systole?

options.explanation: The 'a' wave in atrial pressure tracing is due to atrial contraction.
The 'c' wave is due to bulging of AV valve into atrium during ventricular contraction.
The 'v' wave is due to venous filling of atrium against closed AV valve.
The 'x' descent is due to atrial relaxation and downward displacement of AV valve.
The 'y' descent occurs after AV valve opening.

explanation.overview: The 'a' wave in atrial pressure tracing is due to atrial contraction.
explanation.highYield: JVP waves: a (atrial contraction), c (carotid/ventricular contraction), v (venous filling). x and y descents.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Absent a waves in atrial fibrillation. Large a waves ('cannon waves') in AV dissociation (e.g., complete heart block).

questions.question: Isovolumetric contraction occurs between:

options.text: AV valve closure and semilunar valve opening
options.explanation: All valves are closed during isovolumetric contraction, while pressure rises rapidly.

options.text: Semilunar valve closure and AV valve opening
QRS onset and AV valve closure
options.explanation: AV valve closure occurs after QRS onset.

options.text: T wave end and next P wave

explanation.overview: All valves are closed during isovolumetric contraction, while pressure rises rapidly.
explanation.highYield: Isovolumetric contraction: starts with AV valve closure, ends with semilunar valve opening. Pressure rises, volume constant. Corresponds to S1.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Impaired contractility prolongs isovolumetric contraction, reducing ejection time.

questions.question: The dicrotic notch on the aortic pressure trace corresponds to:

options.explanation: The dicrotic notch (incisura) marks aortic valve closure.
Mitral valve opening follows isovolumetric relaxation.
Rapid ejection follows aortic valve opening.
The notch occurs at the start of isovolumetric relaxation.

explanation.overview: The dicrotic notch (incisura) marks aortic valve closure.
explanation.highYield: Dicrotic notch = aortic valve closure, seen on aortic pressure trace. Corresponds to S2.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Loss of the dicrotic notch can be seen in aortic regurgitation (wide pulse pressure) or severe heart failure.

questions.question: During exercise, cardiac output increases primarily due to:

options.text: Increased heart rate and stroke volume
options.explanation: Both HR and SV increase to raise CO during exercise.
SV also increases, especially in trained individuals.
Afterload may decrease due to vasodilation in exercising muscle, but CO increase is mainly HR and SV.
CVP may increase but not the primary driver.

explanation.overview: Both HR and SV increase to raise CO during exercise.
explanation.highYield: Exercise: ↑ CO = ↑ HR + ↑ SV. SV increase via enhanced venous return (muscle pump), venoconstriction, ↑ contractility.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Maximal CO can reach 20-35 L/min in elite athletes.

questions.question: Mean arterial pressure (MAP) is approximated by:

options.explanation: Not accurate; systole is shorter than diastole.

explanation.overview: MAP = DBP + 1/3 (SBP – DBP).
explanation.highYield: MAP = CO × TPR. Normal MAP ~70-100 mm Hg. Organ perfusion depends on MAP.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: MAP <60-65 mm Hg may compromise cerebral and renal perfusion.

questions.question: Pulse pressure is defined as:

options.text: Mean arterial pressure minus diastolic pressure
options.explanation: That is part of MAP calculation.

explanation.overview: Pulse pressure = SBP – DBP.
explanation.highYield: Pulse pressure reflects stroke volume and arterial compliance. Increased in aortic regurgitation, hyperthyroidism. Decreased in aortic stenosis, tamponade.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Wide pulse pressure is a classic sign of aortic regurgitation.

questions.question: Which vessel has the largest total cross‑sectional area?

options.explanation: Capillaries, though each tiny, have the greatest total cross‑sectional area due to sheer number.
Arterioles are small but total area less than capillaries.

explanation.overview: Capillaries, though each tiny, have the greatest total cross‑sectional area due to sheer number.
explanation.highYield: Total cross‑sectional area: Capillaries > arterioles > veins > arteries. Velocity inversely proportional to area (slowest in capillaries for exchange).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Large capillary surface area facilitates efficient nutrient/waste exchange.

questions.question: The greatest resistance to blood flow occurs in:

options.explanation: Arterioles are the primary resistance vessels due to their small diameter and smooth muscle control.
Capillaries have high total area, lower resistance.
Veins are capacitance vessels, low resistance.

explanation.overview: Arterioles are the primary resistance vessels due to their small diameter and smooth muscle control.
explanation.highYield: Arterioles = resistance vessels. Regulate blood flow and MAP. Innervated by sympathetic nerves (α1 receptors → vasoconstriction).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Arteriolar constriction increases TPR and MAP; vasodilators (e.g., hydralazine) act primarily on arterioles.

questions.question: Poiseuille's law states that flow is proportional to:

options.explanation: Flow ∝ ΔP × r^4 / (8ηL) – small changes in radius greatly affect flow.
It is radius to the fourth power.

explanation.overview: Flow ∝ ΔP × r^4 / (8ηL) – small changes in radius greatly affect flow.
explanation.highYield: R = 8ηL / (πr^4). Halving radius increases resistance 16-fold. Arterioles are key control points.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Atherosclerotic narrowing even by 50% dramatically reduces flow reserve, causing ischemia under stress.

questions.question: Vasodilation of arterioles decreases:

options.explanation: Decreased resistance (due to dilation) increases flow to downstream capillaries.
Dilation may actually increase capillary pressure downstream.

explanation.overview: Decreased resistance (due to dilation) increases flow to downstream capillaries.
explanation.highYield: Arteriolar dilation → ↓ resistance → ↑ flow. Local metabolites (adenosine, CO2, lactic acid) mediate this.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: In sepsis, excessive vasodilation leads to hypotension and distributive shock.

questions.question: Capillary exchange of solutes occurs primarily by:

options.explanation: Diffusion is the most important mechanism for solute exchange across capillary walls.
Filtration is important for fluid movement, not solute exchange.
Bulk flow is for fluid, not solute.

explanation.overview: Diffusion is the most important mechanism for solute exchange across capillary walls.
explanation.highYield: Lipid‑soluble solutes (O2, CO2) diffuse directly. Water‑soluble solutes (glucose, amino acids) pass through pores/fenestrations.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: In inflammation, capillary permeability increases, allowing protein leakage and edema.

questions.question: The force that drives fluid out of capillaries at the arterial end is:

options.explanation: Capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc) exceeds opposing forces, favoring filtration.
Normally near zero or slightly negative.
This opposes filtration, drawing fluid in.
Net filtration pressure is the sum of forces, but the driving force out is Pc.

explanation.overview: Capillary hydrostatic pressure (Pc) exceeds opposing forces, favoring filtration.
explanation.highYield: Starling forces: NFP = (Pc - Pi) - σ(πc - πi). Pc at arteriolar end ~35 mm Hg → filtration. At venous end, Pc ~15 mm Hg → reabsorption.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Increased Pc (e.g., heart failure) leads to pulmonary edema.

questions.question: The primary force promoting fluid reabsorption at the venous end is:

options.explanation: Plasma oncotic pressure (πp) draws fluid back into the capillary.
Pc falls along the capillary, allowing πp to dominate at venous end.
Lymphatic system drains excess fluid, not the primary reabsorption force.

explanation.overview: Plasma oncotic pressure (πp) draws fluid back into the capillary.
explanation.highYield: πp ~25 mm Hg, mainly from albumin. Decreased in liver disease, nephrotic syndrome, malnutrition → edema.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Hypoalbuminemia leads to peripheral edema due to reduced oncotic pressure.

questions.question: Edema can result from:

options.explanation: Causes include heart failure, venous obstruction.

explanation.overview: Any factor that upsets Starling forces can cause edema.
explanation.highYield: Causes of edema: ↑ Pc (HF, venous obstruction), ↓ πc (hypoalbuminemia), lymphatic obstruction, ↑ permeability (inflammation).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Pitting edema is characteristic of increased hydrostatic pressure; non‑pitting suggests lymphatic or protein‑rich edema.

questions.question: The baroreceptor reflex is initiated by changes in:

options.explanation: Baroreceptors in carotid sinus and aortic arch detect stretch from arterial pressure changes.
Atrial volume receptors affect ADH and ANP release.

explanation.overview: Baroreceptors in carotid sinus and aortic arch detect stretch from arterial pressure changes.
explanation.highYield: Carotid sinus → glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) → medulla. Aortic arch → vagus nerve (CN X) → medulla. Regulate short‑term BP.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Carotid sinus hypersensitivity can cause syncope with neck pressure (e.g., shaving, tight collar).

questions.question: An increase in arterial pressure activates baroreceptors, leading to:

options.text: Increased parasympathetic and decreased sympathetic activity
options.explanation: High pressure triggers vagal activation and sympathetic inhibition, lowering HR and vasodilation.

options.text: Increased sympathetic and decreased parasympathetic activity

explanation.overview: High pressure triggers vagal activation and sympathetic inhibition, lowering HR and vasodilation.
explanation.highYield: Baroreflex: ↑ BP → ↑ baroreceptor firing → NTS → ↑ vagal (↓ HR), ↓ sympathetic (↓ HR, ↓ contractility, vasodilation) → BP normalizes.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Baroreflex failure (e.g., after neck radiation) causes labile hypertension.

questions.question: The Bainbridge reflex refers to:

options.text: Increased heart rate in response to increased atrial pressure
options.explanation: Atrial stretch receptors increase HR via vagal afferents and sympathetic activation.

options.text: Decreased heart rate in response to increased atrial pressure

explanation.overview: Atrial stretch receptors increase HR via vagal afferents and sympathetic activation.
explanation.highYield: Bainbridge reflex: ↑ atrial pressure → ↑ HR. Helps match CO to venous return. Involves sympathetic activation.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: May contribute to tachycardia in heart failure or volume overload.

questions.question: The Cushing reflex (Cushing's triad) includes:

options.explanation: Increased ICP causes hypertension, bradycardia, and respiratory irregularity due to brainstem ischemia.
That is more typical of shock.

explanation.overview: Increased ICP causes hypertension, bradycardia, and respiratory irregularity due to brainstem ischemia.
explanation.highYield: Cushing reflex: ↑ ICP → brainstem ischemia → massive sympathetic discharge → hypertension (↑ MAP to perfuse brain) → reflex bradycardia via baroreceptors. Respiratory irregularity.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Cushing's triad is a late sign of increased intracranial pressure, indicating impending brain herniation.

questions.question: Central venous pressure (CVP) is normally about:

options.explanation: Normal CVP ranges from 0 to 8 mm Hg.

explanation.overview: Normal CVP ranges from 0 to 8 mm Hg.
explanation.highYield: CVP = right atrial pressure. Reflects right heart function and intravascular volume. Low CVP: hypovolemia. High CVP: fluid overload, RV failure, tamponade.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: CVP monitoring guides fluid therapy; trend is more important than single values.

questions.question: Elevated CVP may indicate:

options.explanation: Right heart failure increases CVP due to reduced right ventricular output.

explanation.overview: Right heart failure increases CVP due to reduced right ventricular output.
explanation.highYield: High CVP causes: RV failure, pulmonary hypertension, tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade, volume overload.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Jugular venous distention is the bedside correlate of elevated CVP.

questions.question: The Valsalva maneuver involves forced expiration against a closed glottis, causing:

options.text: Increased intrathoracic pressure, decreased venous return, and reflex tachycardia
options.explanation: Raised intrathoracic pressure impedes venous return, dropping BP and triggering reflex tachycardia.

options.text: Decreased intrathoracic pressure and increased CO

options.explanation: CVP may increase initially, but venous return decreases; tachycardia is characteristic.

explanation.overview: Raised intrathoracic pressure impedes venous return, dropping BP and triggering reflex tachycardia.
explanation.highYield: Valsalva phases: Phase I (strain onset) – BP rises; Phase II – ↓ VR → ↓ BP, ↑ HR; Phase III (release) – ↓ BP; Phase IV – overshoot BP, ↓ HR.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: The Valsalva maneuver can terminate supraventricular tachycardia by increasing vagal tone.

questions.question: Pulsus paradoxus is defined as:

options.text: An abnormally large drop in systolic BP during inspiration (>10 mm Hg)
options.explanation: Pulsus paradoxus occurs in cardiac tamponade, severe asthma, etc., due to exaggerated inspiratory fall.

options.text: A rise in systolic BP during inspiration
A drop in diastolic BP during expiration

options.explanation: Can occur but not the definition.

explanation.overview: Pulsus paradoxus occurs in cardiac tamponade, severe asthma, etc., due to exaggerated inspiratory fall.
explanation.highYield: Pulsus paradoxus = >10 mm Hg fall in SBP during normal inspiration. Measured with sphygmomanometer. Caused by exaggerated ventricular interdependence.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Pulsus paradoxus is a key finding in cardiac tamponade (Beck's triad: hypotension, muffled heart sounds, JVD).

questions.question: Coronary blood flow occurs mainly during:

options.explanation: During systole, myocardial compression impedes flow, especially in the left ventricle; flow peaks in diastole.
Systole compresses coronary vessels, reducing flow.
Flow begins to increase but peaks in diastole.

explanation.overview: During systole, myocardial compression impedes flow, especially in the left ventricle; flow peaks in diastole.
explanation.highYield: Coronary perfusion pressure = aortic diastolic pressure – LVEDP. LV receives most flow during diastole. Right ventricle receives flow during both systole and diastole due to lower wall stress.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Tachycardia reduces diastolic filling time, decreasing coronary perfusion and potentially worsening ischemia.

questions.question: The primary regulator of coronary blood flow is:

options.explanation: Coronary flow is tightly coupled to myocardial O2 demand via local metabolites.
Sympathetic nerves can cause vasoconstriction (α) but are overridden by metabolic vasodilation.
Endothelial factors contribute but metabolic regulation is primary.

explanation.overview: Coronary flow is tightly coupled to myocardial O2 demand via local metabolites.
explanation.highYield: Adenosine is a key metabolic vasodilator. Hypoxia → adenosine release → vasodilation. Also NO, prostacyclin.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Coronary steal phenomenon: vasodilators may shunt blood from ischemic to normal areas.

questions.question: Adenosine causes coronary vasodilation by acting on:

options.explanation: Adenosine activates A2A receptors on smooth muscle, increasing cAMP and causing relaxation.
Dopamine receptors have minimal coronary effect.

explanation.overview: Adenosine activates A2A receptors on smooth muscle, increasing cAMP and causing relaxation.
explanation.highYield: Adenosine: A1 receptors in AV node (negative dromotropy), A2A in vessels (vasodilation). Used for stress testing and SVT termination.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Adenosine or regadenoson are used in pharmacologic stress tests to induce coronary hyperemia.

questions.question: In the fetal circulation, the ductus arteriosus connects the:

options.explanation: The ductus arteriosus shunts blood from the pulmonary artery to the aorta, bypassing lungs.

options.text: Umbilical vein to inferior vena cava

explanation.overview: The ductus arteriosus shunts blood from the pulmonary artery to the aorta, bypassing lungs.
explanation.highYield: Fetal shunts: foramen ovale (RA→LA), ductus arteriosus (PA→aorta), ductus venosus (umbilical vein→IVC). Bypass non‑functioning lungs.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) after birth causes a continuous machinery murmur.

questions.question: The foramen ovale in the fetus shunts blood from:

options.explanation: Oxygenated blood from the umbilical vein passes through foramen ovale to the left side.

explanation.overview: Oxygenated blood from the umbilical vein passes through foramen ovale to the left side.
explanation.highYield: Foramen ovale: flap‑like opening between atria. Closes after birth when left atrial pressure exceeds right. Patent foramen ovale (PFO) in ~25% adults.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: PFO can allow paradoxical embolism (venous clot → arterial circulation) causing cryptogenic stroke.

questions.question: At birth, closure of the ductus arteriosus is triggered by:

options.text: Increased O2 tension and decreased prostaglandins
options.explanation: Rising PaO2 causes ductal smooth muscle contraction; prostaglandin decline also contributes.
Surfactant affects lung compliance, not ductus.

explanation.overview: Rising PaO2 causes ductal smooth muscle contraction; prostaglandin decline also contributes.
explanation.highYield: Ductus closure: O2‑sensitive K+ channels → depolarization → Ca2+ influx → contraction. Prostaglandin E2 keeps ductus open; NSAIDs (indomethacin) promote closure.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: In ductal‑dependent congenital heart disease, prostaglandin E1 infusion maintains ductus patency.

questions.question: Korotkoff sounds are heard when measuring blood pressure with a sphygmomanometer. Phase I corresponds to:

options.text: The first appearance of clear tapping sounds (systolic pressure)
options.explanation: Phase I marks systolic pressure; phase V (disappearance) is diastolic in adults.
Phase I is systolic in all ages.

explanation.overview: Phase I marks systolic pressure; phase V (disappearance) is diastolic in adults.
explanation.highYield: Korotkoff phases: I (tapping, systolic), II (swishing), III (louder tapping), IV (muffling), V (silence, diastolic).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: In aortic regurgitation, sounds may never disappear (diastolic = phase IV).

questions.question: The pulse pressure is widened in which condition?

options.explanation: Aortic regurgitation increases stroke volume and decreases diastolic pressure, widening pulse pressure.
Mitral stenosis reduces LV filling, lowering SV.

explanation.overview: Aortic regurgitation increases stroke volume and decreases diastolic pressure, widening pulse pressure.
explanation.highYield: Wide pulse pressure causes: aortic regurgitation, patent ductus arteriosus, hyperthyroidism, anemia, aging (stiff arteries).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Bounding pulses and head bobbing (de Musset sign) are signs of wide pulse pressure.

questions.question: A narrow pulse pressure is characteristic of:

options.explanation: Aortic stenosis reduces stroke volume, decreasing pulse pressure.
Fever widens pulse pressure due to vasodilation and increased HR.

explanation.overview: Aortic stenosis reduces stroke volume, decreasing pulse pressure.
explanation.highYield: Narrow pulse pressure causes: aortic stenosis, heart failure, hypovolemia, cardiac tamponade.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Pulsus parvus et tardus (weak and delayed carotid upstroke) is classic for severe aortic stenosis.

questions.question: The formula for cardiac output using the Fick principle is:

options.text: CO = O2 consumption / (arterial O2 content – venous O2 content)
options.explanation: The Fick principle states that CO equals oxygen consumption divided by arteriovenous oxygen difference.

options.text: CO = (arterial O2 content – venous O2 content) / O2 consumption
CO = O2 consumption × arterial O2 content
CO = (venous O2 content – arterial O2 content) × O2 consumption

explanation.overview: The Fick principle states that CO equals oxygen consumption divided by arteriovenous oxygen difference.
explanation.highYield: CO = VO2 / (CaO2 – CvO2). CaO2 – CvO2 = arteriovenous O2 difference. Normal ~4‑5 mL O2/dL. Used in cardiac catheterization.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: In low CO states, oxygen extraction increases, widening A‑V O2 difference and lowering SvO2.

questions.question: Normal mixed venous oxygen saturation (SvO2) is approximately:

explanation.overview: SvO2 normally ~75%, reflecting oxygen extraction.
explanation.highYield: SvO2 = mixed venous O2 saturation (pulmonary artery). Reflects balance between O2 delivery and consumption. Low SvO2: ↓ CO, ↓ Hb, ↓ SaO2, ↑ O2 demand. High SvO2: sepsis, decreased O2 extraction.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: SvO2 <60% indicates impaired tissue oxygenation and is used to guide therapy in shock.

questions.question: Central venous pressure is measured via a catheter placed in the:

options.text: Superior vena cava or right atrium
options.explanation: CVP reflects pressure in the right atrium.
Left atrial pressure is measured indirectly via PAWP.

explanation.overview: CVP reflects pressure in the right atrium.
explanation.highYield: CVP measured by central venous catheter (internal jugular or subclavian). Trends used for volume status.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: CVP is often used as a surrogate for right ventricular preload, but dynamic indices (e.g., IVC collapsibility) are more reliable.

questions.question: Pulmonary artery wedge pressure (PAWP) estimates:

options.explanation: When balloon‑tipped catheter is wedged, it reflects left atrial pressure.
PAP is measured before balloon inflation.
PAWP correlates with LVEDP in absence of mitral valve disease.

explanation.overview: When balloon‑tipped catheter is wedged, it reflects left atrial pressure.
explanation.highYield: PAWP = pulmonary capillary wedge pressure. Normal 6‑12 mm Hg. In mitral stenosis, PAWP > LVEDP. Reflects left‑sided filling pressure.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Elevated PAWP (>18 mm Hg) indicates left‑sided congestion (e.g., heart failure).

questions.question: A raised PAWP is indicative of:

options.explanation: Elevated left atrial pressure (e.g., in LV failure) increases PAWP.
Right HF raises CVP, not PAWP.
Pulmonary hypertension may be secondary to left heart failure.

explanation.overview: Elevated left atrial pressure (e.g., in LV failure) increases PAWP.
explanation.highYield: PAWP >18 mm Hg suggests pulmonary congestion. Used to differentiate cardiogenic from non‑cardiogenic pulmonary edema (ARDS: normal PAWP).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: In cardiogenic shock, PAWP is high; in hypovolemic shock, PAWP is low.

questions.question: The diagram shows a normal left ventricular pressure‑volume loop. Point A represents:

options.explanation: Point A is at the lower right, indicating end‑diastolic volume and pressure.
ESV is at the upper left corner.
That occurs at the upper right.
Mitral valve opens at the lower left.
Start of isovolumetric contraction is lower right but not labeled A typically.

explanation.overview: Point A is at the lower right, indicating end‑diastolic volume and pressure.
explanation.highYield: PV loop: bottom right = EDV (mitral valve closure), top right = aortic valve opening, top left = ESV (aortic valve closure), bottom left = mitral valve opening.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: PV loops provide a load‑independent assessment of ventricular function.

questions.question: In the pressure‑volume loop, the width of the loop represents:

options.explanation: The horizontal distance between EDV and ESV is stroke volume.

explanation.overview: The horizontal distance between EDV and ESV is stroke volume.
explanation.highYield: SV = EDV – ESV. Area inside loop = stroke work (external work).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: A narrow PV loop indicates low stroke volume (e.g., hypovolemia, heart failure).

questions.question: An increase in afterload shifts the PV loop to the:

options.explanation: Higher afterload impairs ejection, increasing ESV and decreasing SV.
Pressure does increase, but the loop also shifts right.

explanation.overview: Higher afterload impairs ejection, increasing ESV and decreasing SV.
explanation.highYield: Increased afterload: taller, narrower loop, shifted right. Decreased afterload: wider, shorter loop, left shift. Important in hypertension and aortic stenosis.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Vasodilators decrease afterload, shifting the loop left and increasing SV.

questions.question: Increased contractility is reflected on the PV loop by:

options.explanation: Positive inotropy ejects more blood, reducing ESV and increasing SV.
Increased contractility shifts the ESPVR upward/leftward.

explanation.overview: Positive inotropy ejects more blood, reducing ESV and increasing SV.
explanation.highYield: Increased contractility: steeper ESPVR slope, increased SV, decreased ESV, leftward shift. Seen with catecholamines.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: In heart failure, contractility is reduced; dobutamine can augment contractility acutely.

questions.question: The dP/dt max is an index of:

options.explanation: Maximum rate of pressure rise during isovolumetric contraction reflects contractility.

explanation.overview: Maximum rate of pressure rise during isovolumetric contraction reflects contractility.
explanation.highYield: dP/dt max: increased by positive inotropes, decreased in heart failure. Measured invasively.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: dP/dt is used in research and critical care to assess changes in contractility.

questions.question: Cardiac work can be divided into external work (stroke work) and:

options.explanation: Total mechanical work is the area inside the PV loop (external) plus the area under the curve (potential).
Isovolumetric work is part of the total.
Kinetic energy is a minor component.

explanation.overview: Total mechanical work is the area inside the PV loop (external) plus the area under the curve (potential).
explanation.highYield: PVA = stroke work + potential energy. MVO2 correlates with PVA. Afterload increases PVA more than preload.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Increasing afterload increases myocardial oxygen consumption disproportionately.

questions.question: Which of the following increases myocardial O2 consumption the most?

options.explanation: Wall tension is a major determinant, but all increase MVO2.
Afterload increases wall tension, raising MVO2.
All major determinants (HR, contractility, wall tension) raise MVO2.

explanation.overview: All major determinants (HR, contractility, wall tension) raise MVO2.
explanation.highYield: Major determinants of MVO2: wall tension (preload × afterload / thickness), contractility, heart rate. Increased wall tension is the most oxygen‑costly.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Beta‑blockers reduce MVO2 by decreasing HR and contractility, beneficial in coronary artery disease.

questions.question: The Law of Laplace for a sphere states that wall tension (T) is:

options.explanation: For a sphere, tension = pressure × radius / 2; for a cylinder, T = P × r.
That is for a cylinder (e.g., blood vessel).

explanation.overview: For a sphere, tension = pressure × radius / 2; for a cylinder, T = P × r.
explanation.highYield: LaPlace: T ∝ P × r. Dilated heart: increased radius → increased wall stress → ↑ MVO2. Hypertrophy decreases stress by increasing wall thickness.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: In dilated cardiomyopathy, increased wall stress worsens function and increases oxygen demand.

questions.question: Ventricular hypertrophy initially compensates for increased afterload by:

options.text: Increasing wall thickness to normalize wall stress
options.explanation: Hypertrophy adds sarcomeres, reducing wall tension per unit area (LaPlace).
Concentric hypertrophy may reduce cavity size, but the primary mechanism is wall thickening.

explanation.overview: Hypertrophy adds sarcomeres, reducing wall tension per unit area (LaPlace).
explanation.highYield: Concentric hypertrophy (pressure overload, e.g., AS, HTN): parallel sarcomere addition, wall thickens, normalizes stress. Eccentric hypertrophy (volume overload, e.g., AR): series sarcomere addition, chamber enlarges.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Eventually, hypertrophy becomes maladaptive, leading to diastolic dysfunction and heart failure.

questions.question: In dilated cardiomyopathy, wall stress is increased because:

options.text: Radius is enlarged without proportional wall thickening
options.explanation: Laplace: tension ∝ P × r / thickness; increased r raises tension, worsening function.
Pressure may be normal or low.
In dilated cardiomyopathy, wall thickness is relatively normal but cavity is enlarged.

explanation.overview: Laplace: tension ∝ P × r / thickness; increased r raises tension, worsening function.
explanation.highYield: Dilated cardiomyopathy: ↑ radius → ↑ wall stress → ↑ MVO2 → further dysfunction. Afterload mismatch worsens ejection.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Ventricular dilation is a poor prognostic sign in heart failure.

questions.question: End‑systolic pressure‑volume relationship (ESPVR) is a load‑independent measure of:

options.explanation: ESPVR slope (Ees) increases with enhanced contractility.

explanation.overview: ESPVR slope (Ees) increases with enhanced contractility.
explanation.highYield: ESPVR = line connecting end‑systolic points at different afterloads. Slope = Ees (contractility). Steeper slope = increased contractility.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: ESPVR is relatively load‑independent, making it a gold standard for assessing contractility in research.

questions.question: The end‑diastolic pressure‑volume relationship (EDPVR) reflects:

options.explanation: EDPVR curve describes passive filling properties; steeper slope means less compliance.
EDPVR influences filling, which affects SV.

explanation.overview: EDPVR curve describes passive filling properties; steeper slope means less compliance.
explanation.highYield: EDPVR = relationship between end‑diastolic pressure and volume. Shifted up/left in diastolic dysfunction (stiff ventricle). Flatter in dilated cardiomyopathy.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: HFpEF is characterized by a stiff ventricle with upward/leftward shift of EDPVR.

questions.question: In heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF), the EDPVR is typically:

options.explanation: HFpEF involves diastolic dysfunction with stiff ventricles.
More compliant ventricle would be flatter.

explanation.overview: HFpEF involves diastolic dysfunction with stiff ventricles.
explanation.highYield: HFpEF: increased passive stiffness → left/upward shifted EDPVR → ↑ filling pressures → pulmonary congestion. Normal or near‑normal EF.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Diastolic dysfunction can be detected by echocardiography (E/e' ratio, left atrial volume).

questions.question: The phenomenon of 'Anrep effect' refers to:

options.text: Slow increase in contractility after an abrupt increase in afterload
options.explanation: The Anrep effect is a delayed inotropic response to increased afterload, possibly via Na+/Ca2+ exchange.

options.text: Immediate increase in contractility with stretch
Decrease in contractility with increased afterload
Increase in heart rate with increased preload

explanation.overview: The Anrep effect is a delayed inotropic response to increased afterload, possibly via Na+/Ca2+ exchange.
explanation.highYield: Anrep effect: afterload increase → initial ↓ SV → then gradual recovery via ↑ Ca2+ transients (intracellular Na+ accumulation). Helps maintain CO.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: May play a role in compensation during acute hypertension.

questions.question: The 'Bowditch effect' (Treppe) is:

options.text: Increase in contractility with increased heart rate
options.explanation: Higher frequency allows more Ca2+ entry and accumulation, increasing contractility.

options.text: Decrease in contractility with increased heart rate
Increase in force with increased preload
Decrease in force with increased afterload
Staircase phenomenon due to increased Ca2+ accumulation
options.explanation: This describes the mechanism but the effect is increased contractility with HR; the original answer likely intended 'Increase in contractility with increased heart rate'. We'll map to A as correct.

explanation.overview: Higher frequency allows more Ca2+ entry and accumulation, increasing contractility.
explanation.highYield: Bowditch/Treppe: positive force‑frequency relationship. ↑ HR → ↑ contractility (more Ca2+ loading). In heart failure, this relationship may be blunted or negative.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: In heart failure, tachycardia may not increase contractility, contributing to decompensation.

questions.question: The velocity of circumferential fiber shortening (Vcf) is an index of:

options.explanation: Vcf reflects how fast the ventricle shortens, independent of load to some extent.

explanation.overview: Vcf reflects how fast the ventricle shortens, independent of load to some extent.
explanation.highYield: Vcf (circumferential fiber shortening velocity) decreases with reduced contractility. Can be measured by echocardiography.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: A stress‑corrected Vcf can be used to detect subtle contractile abnormalities.

questions.question: Normal cardiac output for an average adult at rest is approximately:

explanation.overview: Cardiac output ≈ 5 L/min at rest.
explanation.highYield: CO = 4-8 L/min at rest. Can increase 4-5 fold during exercise.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Low cardiac output syndrome: CO < 2 L/min/m², causing organ hypoperfusion.

questions.question: Cardiac index (CI) is cardiac output normalized to:

explanation.overview: CI = CO / BSA (normal ~2.5‑4 L/min/m²).
explanation.highYield: Cardiac index accounts for body size. Normal CI > 2.2 L/min/m².
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: CI is used to guide therapy in shock; a low CI indicates need for inotropes or fluids.

questions.question: Total peripheral resistance (TPR) is calculated as:

options.explanation: TPR = (MAP – CVP) / CO, often approximated as MAP/CO.

explanation.overview: TPR = (MAP – CVP) / CO, often approximated as MAP/CO.
explanation.highYield: TPR = (MAP – CVP) / CO. Normal ~800‑1200 dynes·sec·cm⁻⁵. Systemic vascular resistance (SVR) is used interchangeably.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: High SVR in cardiogenic shock, low SVR in septic shock.

questions.question: Vascular compliance is highest in:

options.explanation: Veins are highly compliant capacitance vessels, holding most of the blood volume.
Arterioles have muscular walls, low compliance.
Aorta is elastic, but veins are more compliant.

explanation.overview: Veins are highly compliant capacitance vessels, holding most of the blood volume.
explanation.highYield: Compliance = ΔV / ΔP. Veins have 20‑30 times the compliance of arteries. Act as volume reservoir.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Venoconstriction (e.g., sympathetic activation) mobilizes blood, increasing venous return.

questions.question: The majority of blood volume (~60‑70%) is contained in the:

explanation.overview: Veins serve as a reservoir.
explanation.highYield: Blood volume distribution: systemic veins ~64%, systemic arteries ~13%, pulmonary circulation ~9%, heart ~7%, capillaries ~7%.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Venodilators (e.g., nitroglycerin) reduce preload by increasing venous capacitance.

questions.question: Sympathetic stimulation causes venoconstriction, which:

options.explanation: Venoconstriction mobilizes blood from reservoirs, increasing VR and EDV.

options.text: Has no effect on venous return

explanation.overview: Venoconstriction mobilizes blood from reservoirs, increasing VR and EDV.
explanation.highYield: Venous system: α1 receptors mediate constriction. Venoconstriction shifts volume from unstressed to stressed, increasing CVP and VR.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: In hemorrhage, sympathetic venoconstriction helps maintain cardiac output.

questions.question: The respiratory pump aids venous return during inspiration by:

options.text: Decreasing intrathoracic pressure, drawing blood into thoracic veins
options.explanation: Negative intrathoracic pressure increases the pressure gradient for venous return.
Abdominal compression is part of the muscle pump.
Diaphragm contraction decreases intrathoracic pressure, but the overall effect is the pressure gradient.

explanation.overview: Negative intrathoracic pressure increases the pressure gradient for venous return.
explanation.highYield: Inspiration: ↓ intrathoracic pressure → ↑ venous return → ↑ RV filling → ↑ RV output. Expiration: opposite. This contributes to respiratory variation in stroke volume.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: In tamponade, Kussmaul sign: lack of inspiratory fall in CVP due to impaired filling.

questions.question: The skeletal muscle pump promotes venous return by:

options.text: Compressing veins and forcing blood toward heart, with valves preventing backflow
options.explanation: Contraction squeezes veins, and valves ensure one‑way flow.
Vasodilation occurs in muscle but the pump is mechanical.

explanation.overview: Contraction squeezes veins, and valves ensure one‑way flow.
explanation.highYield: Skeletal muscle pump: during walking, venous pressure drops due to emptying of venous compartments. Valves prevent reflux. Important for upright posture.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Venous insufficiency or valve incompetence leads to varicose veins and edema.

questions.question: A decrease in plasma volume (hypovolemia) initially causes:

options.text: Decreased venous return and decreased CO
options.explanation: Low blood volume reduces VR, lowering EDV and CO via Frank‑Starling.

options.text: Increased venous return and increased CO

options.explanation: Contractility may increase via sympathetic reflex.

explanation.overview: Low blood volume reduces VR, lowering EDV and CO via Frank‑Starling.
explanation.highYield: Hypovolemia → ↓ VR → ↓ EDV → ↓ SV → ↓ CO → ↓ BP → baroreflex → ↑ HR, ↑ contractility, vasoconstriction.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Tachycardia is a compensatory response to hypovolemia; fluid resuscitation restores CO.

questions.question: The most important long‑term regulator of arterial pressure is:

options.explanation: RAAS controls blood volume and vascular tone over hours to days.
ANP opposes RAAS but is not the primary long‑term regulator.
ADH contributes but RAAS is dominant.

explanation.overview: RAAS controls blood volume and vascular tone over hours to days.
explanation.highYield: RAAS: renin (kidney) → Ang I → Ang II (ACE) → vasoconstriction, aldosterone (Na+ retention), thirst, ADH release. Long‑term BP control via fluid balance.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are cornerstone therapies for hypertension and heart failure.

questions.question: Angiotensin II causes:

options.explanation: Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor and stimulates aldosterone, ADH, and thirst.
It constricts efferent arteriole, maintaining GFR in low flow, but decreases overall renal blood flow.

explanation.overview: Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor and stimulates aldosterone, ADH, and thirst.
explanation.highYield: Ang II: potent vasoconstrictor, ↑ aldosterone → Na+ retention, ↑ thirst, ↑ ADH, ↑ sympathetic tone. Also promotes cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: ACE inhibitors block Ang II formation, lowering BP and providing cardiorenal protection.

questions.question: Atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP) is released in response to:

options.explanation: ANP is secreted from atrial myocytes when stretched, promoting natriuresis and vasodilation.
ANP is released in response to stretch.
Ang II stimulates aldosterone, not ANP.

explanation.overview: ANP is secreted from atrial myocytes when stretched, promoting natriuresis and vasodilation.
explanation.highYield: ANP: released by atrial distension → ↑ cGMP → natriuresis, vasodilation, ↓ renin, ↓ aldosterone. Counter‑regulatory to RAAS. BNP from ventricles.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: BNP (or NT‑proBNP) is a diagnostic biomarker for heart failure.

questions.question: Nitric oxide (NO) causes vasodilation by:

options.text: Increasing cGMP in smooth muscle, reducing Ca2+ sensitivity
options.explanation: NO activates guanylyl cyclase, increasing cGMP, which leads to relaxation.
Part of the pathway, but the ultimate effect is increased cGMP.
NO activates soluble guanylyl cyclase, increasing cGMP, which leads to relaxation via multiple mechanisms including decreased Ca2+ sensitivity and hyperpolarization.

explanation.overview: NO activates soluble guanylyl cyclase, increasing cGMP, which leads to relaxation.
explanation.highYield: NO: from eNOS in endothelium, diffuses to smooth muscle, activates sGC → ↑ cGMP → PKG activation → relaxation. Mediated by shear stress, acetylcholine, etc.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Nitrates (nitroglycerin) are NO donors; sildenafil potentiates NO by inhibiting PDE5.

questions.question: Endothelin‑1 is a potent:

options.explanation: Endothelin, released from endothelium, causes powerful, long‑lasting vasoconstriction.
It may have some inotropic effect, but primarily a vasoconstrictor.

explanation.overview: Endothelin, released from endothelium, causes powerful, long‑lasting vasoconstriction.
explanation.highYield: Endothelin‑1: ETA receptor (smooth muscle) → vasoconstriction, proliferation. ETB receptor (endothelial) → NO release. Imbalance in pulmonary hypertension.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Endothelin receptor antagonists (bosentan, ambrisentan) are used in pulmonary arterial hypertension.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a local vasodilator metabolite?

options.explanation: Angiotensin II is a systemic vasoconstrictor; the others are local metabolites that cause vasodilation.

explanation.overview: Angiotensin II is a systemic vasoconstrictor; the others are local metabolites that cause vasodilation.
explanation.highYield: Local vasodilators: adenosine, K+, H+, CO2, lactic acid, hypoxia. Local vasoconstrictors: endothelin, thromboxane A2.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Metabolic vasodilation matches blood flow to tissue demand (active hyperemia).

questions.question: Reactive hyperemia refers to:

options.text: Increased flow after a period of ischemia
options.explanation: Occlusion causes metabolite accumulation; upon release, flow transiently exceeds baseline.
Flow increases after exercise, not decreases.

explanation.overview: Occlusion causes metabolite accumulation; upon release, flow transiently exceeds baseline.
explanation.highYield: Reactive hyperemia: repayment of O2 debt and washout of metabolites. Duration and peak flow correlate with occlusion time.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Used clinically in assessing peripheral artery disease and coronary flow reserve.

questions.question: Active hyperemia is the increase in blood flow due to:

options.explanation: Local metabolites match flow to metabolic demand.
Inflammation increases flow but active hyperemia refers to metabolic.

explanation.overview: Local metabolites match flow to metabolic demand.
explanation.highYield: Active hyperemia: ↑ metabolism → ↓ O2, ↑ CO2, ↑ K+, adenosine → vasodilation → ↑ flow. Examples: exercising skeletal muscle, brain.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Coronary artery disease prevents adequate active hyperemia, causing ischemia during exertion.

questions.question: Autoregulation of blood flow means that flow remains relatively constant despite changes in:

options.explanation: Organs like kidney and brain maintain constant flow over a range of pressures via myogenic and metabolic mechanisms.
Sympathetic influence is overridden within the autoregulatory range.
Viscosity affects flow but not autoregulation.

explanation.overview: Organs like kidney and brain maintain constant flow over a range of pressures via myogenic and metabolic mechanisms.
explanation.highYield: Autoregulation range: MAP ~50-150 mm Hg in cerebral, 80-180 mm Hg in renal. Mechanisms: myogenic (stretch‑induced constriction) and metabolic (tissue demand).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Loss of autoregulation in acute brain injury makes cerebral flow dependent on systemic pressure.

questions.question: The myogenic response refers to:

options.text: Vascular smooth muscle contraction in response to stretch
options.explanation: Increased pressure stretches arterioles, causing them to constrict to maintain flow.

options.text: Vascular relaxation in response to stretch

explanation.overview: Increased pressure stretches arterioles, causing them to constrict to maintain flow.
explanation.highYield: Myogenic response: stretch‑activated channels → depolarization → Ca2+ influx → constriction. Contributes to autoregulation. Opposed by metabolic vasodilation.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: In hypertension, the myogenic response may shift to a higher pressure range.

questions.question: Shear stress on endothelium stimulates release of:

options.explanation: Shear stress activates eNOS, releasing NO.
Shear stress releases NO and prostacyclin, causing vasodilation.

explanation.overview: Shear stress releases NO and prostacyclin, causing vasodilation.
explanation.highYield: Flow‑mediated dilation: ↑ flow → ↑ shear → eNOS activation → NO release → vasodilation. Tested in brachial artery for endothelial function.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Impaired flow‑mediated dilation is an early marker of endothelial dysfunction and atherosclerosis.

questions.question: The baroreceptors are most sensitive to:

options.explanation: Baroreceptors respond to both magnitude and rate of change.

explanation.overview: Baroreceptors respond to both magnitude and rate of change.
explanation.highYield: Baroreceptors are rapidly adapting, sensitive to dP/dt. Firing rate increases with steeper pressure rise. Located in carotid sinus and aortic arch.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Loss of baroreflex sensitivity occurs in aging and diabetes, leading to orthostatic hypotension.

questions.question: In chronic hypertension, baroreceptors:

options.text: Reset to operate at higher pressure
options.explanation: Baroreceptors adapt to sustained high pressure by resetting their set point.
They continue functioning but at a higher threshold.

explanation.overview: Baroreceptors adapt to sustained high pressure by resetting their set point.
explanation.highYield: Baroreceptor resetting: in chronic HTN, baroreceptors shift their operating range upward, maintaining normal buffering function but at higher pressures.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Resetting prevents appropriate BP lowering; contributes to maintenance of hypertension.

questions.question: Chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies are primarily sensitive to:

options.text: Low O2, high CO2, low pH
options.explanation: Peripheral chemoreceptors detect hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and acidosis.

explanation.overview: Peripheral chemoreceptors detect hypoxemia, hypercapnia, and acidosis.
explanation.highYield: Carotid body (CN IX) and aortic body (CN X). Respond to ↓ PaO2 (<60 mmHg), ↑ PaCO2, ↓ pH. Stimulate sympathetic outflow → ↑ BP, ↑ HR (unless severe hypoxia → bradycardia).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: In sleep apnea, intermittent hypoxia stimulates chemoreceptors, contributing to hypertension.

questions.question: Stimulation of peripheral chemoreceptors by severe hypoxia causes:

options.explanation: In severe hypoxia, chemoreflex can cause bradycardia and peripheral vasoconstriction (diving reflex).
That is the response to moderate hypoxia via hyperventilation‑induced lung reflexes; severe hypoxia causes bradycardia.
Vagal tone is part of the bradycardia response.

explanation.overview: In severe hypoxia, chemoreflex can cause bradycardia and peripheral vasoconstriction (diving reflex).
explanation.highYield: Primary chemoreflex: ↑ ventilation, ↑ sympathetic → vasoconstriction. In severe hypoxia, direct effect on heart → bradycardia. Combined with vasoconstriction (diving reflex) to preserve O2 for brain/heart.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: The diving reflex is used therapeutically to terminate supraventricular tachycardia (cold water to face).

questions.question: The Bezold‑Jarisch reflex involves:

options.text: Bradycardia, hypotension, and apnea in response to chemicals in the ventricle
options.explanation: Stimulation of cardiac chemoreceptors (e.g., by veratridine) causes this inhibitory reflex.

explanation.overview: Stimulation of cardiac chemoreceptors (e.g., by veratridine) causes this inhibitory reflex.
explanation.highYield: Bezold‑Jarisch reflex: ventricular chemoreceptors → vagal C‑fibers → medulla → profound bradycardia, hypotension, apnea. Mediated by serotonin, bradykinin, etc. May contribute to vasovagal syncope.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: This reflex can be triggered by myocardial ischemia or reperfusion, causing sudden bradycardia and hypotension.

questions.question: In a patient with heart failure, the compensatory increase in sympathetic tone initially:

options.text: Maintains cardiac output but increases afterload
options.explanation: Sympathetic activation supports CO but also raises TPR, increasing workload.
Preload may increase due to fluid retention.

explanation.overview: Sympathetic activation supports CO but also raises TPR, increasing workload.
explanation.highYield: Heart failure compensation: ↑ sympathetic → ↑ HR, contractility, vasoconstriction. Initially beneficial but long‑term leads to maladaptive remodeling. Beta‑blockers improve survival.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Carvedilol, metoprolol succinate, bisoprolol reduce mortality in HFrEF.

questions.question: A third heart sound (S3) is often heard in:

options.explanation: S3 can be physiologic in children/young adults or pathologic in heart failure.
S3 can be physiologic in young or pathologic in heart failure.

explanation.overview: S3 can be physiologic in children/young adults or pathologic in heart failure.
explanation.highYield: S3 = ventricular gallop, occurs early diastole. Physiologic in <40 years. Pathologic: heart failure (elevated filling pressures), constrictive pericarditis.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: S3 is a sensitive but not specific sign of systolic heart failure.

questions.question: A fourth heart sound (S4) is caused by:

options.text: Atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle
options.explanation: S4 occurs just after P wave in conditions like hypertrophy, where atria contract forcefully.

explanation.overview: S4 occurs just after P wave in conditions like hypertrophy, where atria contract forcefully.
explanation.highYield: S4 = atrial gallop, late diastole. Always pathologic. Indicates decreased ventricular compliance (HTN, AS, HCM, CAD).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: S4 is heard just before S1, producing a 'Ten‑nes‑see' rhythm (S4‑S1‑S2).

questions.question: Pulsus alternans is a pattern of alternating strong and weak beats seen in:

options.explanation: Alternating contractility due to impaired Ca2+ handling occurs in LV dysfunction.
AR causes wide pulse pressure, not alternans.
MS does not cause pulsus alternans.

explanation.overview: Alternating contractility due to impaired Ca2+ handling occurs in LV dysfunction.
explanation.highYield: Pulsus alternans: beat‑to‑beat variation in stroke volume. Sign of severe left ventricular failure. Often accompanied by S3.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Detectable by palpation or sphygmomanometry; associated with poor prognosis.

questions.question: The most common cause of right heart failure is:

options.explanation: Left HF increases pulmonary pressures, leading to right HF.
Pulmonary HTN can be primary or secondary to left HF.
PE causes acute right heart strain.
TR is often secondary to right ventricular dilation.

explanation.overview: Left HF increases pulmonary pressures, leading to right HF.
explanation.highYield: Most common cause of right heart failure is left heart failure (passive backward transmission of pressure). Isolated right HF less common (cor pulmonale, primary pulmonary hypertension).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Signs of right HF: JVD, peripheral edema, hepatomegaly, ascites.

questions.question: Jugular venous distention is a sign of:

options.explanation: Elevated CVP in right HF causes JVD.
Left HF alone may not cause JVD until right HF develops.
AS does not directly affect JVP.
MR may eventually lead to pulmonary HTN and right HF.

explanation.overview: Elevated CVP in right HF causes JVD.
explanation.highYield: JVD = visible distended neck veins at >45° angle. Reflects elevated right atrial pressure. Differential includes: right HF, pulmonary HTN, tamponade, constrictive pericarditis, SVC syndrome.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Hepatojugular reflux: pressure on liver increases JVP, indicating right HF.

questions.question: Kussmaul sign (increased JVP during inspiration) is characteristic of:

options.explanation: In constrictive pericarditis, inspiratory fall in intrathoracic pressure fails to transmit to heart, causing JVP rise.
Tamponade typically shows a prominent x descent, not Kussmaul.
RV infarct causes elevated JVP but not necessarily Kussmaul.
HF does not typically show Kussmaul sign.

explanation.overview: In constrictive pericarditis, inspiratory fall in intrathoracic pressure fails to transmit to heart, causing JVP rise.
explanation.highYield: Kussmaul sign: paradoxical rise in JVP during inspiration. Causes: constrictive pericarditis, restrictive cardiomyopathy, right ventricular infarction.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Kussmaul sign helps differentiate constrictive pericarditis from cardiac tamponade (tamponade has pulsus paradoxus, not Kussmaul).

questions.question: Pulsus paradoxus is defined as a drop in systolic BP >10 mmHg during inspiration. It is classically seen in:

options.explanation: Tamponade exaggerates inspiratory fall due to ventricular interdependence.
AR does not cause pulsus paradoxus.
HCM has its own dynamic findings.
PE may cause acute right heart strain but not classic pulsus paradoxus.

explanation.overview: Tamponade exaggerates inspiratory fall due to ventricular interdependence.
explanation.highYield: Pulsus paradoxus: inspiratory drop in SBP >10 mmHg. Classic for cardiac tamponade. Also severe asthma/COPD, constrictive pericarditis (less common).
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: In tamponade, Beck's triad: hypotension, muffled heart sounds, JVD. Pulsus paradoxus confirms.

questions.question: The normal PR interval duration is:

explanation.overview: Normal PR interval is 120‑200 ms.
explanation.highYield: PR interval = onset of P to onset of QRS. Represents AV conduction time. Affected by autonomic tone and medications.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: PR >200 ms = first‑degree AV block; <120 ms with delta wave = WPW.

questions.question: The normal QRS duration is:

options.explanation: QRS is typically 80‑100 ms, up to 120 ms.
The upper limit is 120 ms, not 0.12 seconds exactly. The answer '< 0.12 seconds' is more accurate.

explanation.overview: Normal QRS is < 120 ms.
explanation.highYield: QRS duration: normal ≤100 ms in adults, but <120 ms is considered normal. Wide QRS (≥120 ms) = bundle branch block, ventricular rhythm, hyperkalemia, toxicity.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: New left bundle branch block is often indicative of underlying heart disease.

questions.question: A wide QRS (>0.12 s) suggests:

options.text: Bundle branch block or ventricular origin

options.explanation: Ischemia typically affects ST‑T, not QRS width.
Hyperkalemia can widen QRS, but BBB is more common.

explanation.overview: Delayed ventricular conduction widens QRS.
explanation.highYield: Wide QRS differential: bundle branch block, ventricular pacing, ventricular tachycardia, pre‑excitation (WPW), hyperkalemia, tricyclic antidepressant overdose.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: In tachycardia with wide QRS, assume VT until proven otherwise.

questions.question: ST segment elevation on ECG is characteristic of:

explanation.overview: ST elevation can occur in various conditions but is classically seen in STEMI.
explanation.highYield: ST elevation causes: STEMI, pericarditis (diffuse), early repolarization, LV aneurysm, vasospasm, Brugada pattern. Must correlate clinically.
explanation.clinicalCorrelation: Acute STEMI requires emergent reperfusion therapy.

questions.question: Deep, symmetrical T wave inversions may indicate:
